title: Lithuania has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM says
description: Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrend
body: Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad."We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC."We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace."We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."Moscow did not comment on the incident.

schema.headline: Lithuania has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM says

title: The simple skincare routine for teens that actually works - and five expert tips
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years ByCamilla HorroxHealth report
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years ByCamilla HorroxHealth reporterSocial media is driving the trend for "flawless complexions" and complex "glass skin" routines in teenagers, with many prioritising advice from influencers in Get Ready With Me (GRWM) videos over professionals. But do teens really need a multi-step skincare routine?For consultant dermatologist Dr Jonathan Kentley, the most concerning influence social media is having is the "relentless images of unrealistic beauty standards"."I've seen thousands of patients and I've never seen anyone with 'glass skin'. I don't think it exists, and it's just these over-filtered images that make children think that this is achievable when it's not."Visible pores, blackheads, blemishes, pigmentation, redness and scarring are all very normal for teenage skin, says Dr Kentley. But he adds that everyone's normal is different: "I don't think there's anything that is really abnormal."Figure caption, Is our skin care routine actually making it worse?More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years.Dr Zainab Laftah, a consultant dermatologist, explains that most of the so-called problems you encounter during puberty are related to testosterone, which drives rises in oil production and acne.Boys can experience more of these problems, but girls have testosterone as well so get many of the same symptoms."This, together with blocked hair follicles and inflammation, leads to blackheads, whiteheads and inflamed spots," Dr Laftah says. "Acne is very, very common and it's normal and treatable."Salicylic acid, a common active ingredient that penetrates into oil-filled pores to help clear the buildup of sebum and dead skin cells "can be particularly helpful for teenagers with oily or acne-prone skin" says Dr Laftah, warning that unnecessary or excessive use may cause dryness and irritation.If you're suffering from severe acne or a severe skin problem, Dr Kentley advises getting help from your GP or a dermatologist rather than engaging with people on social media on how to manage it.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Social media is fuelling the trend for "flawless complexions" and multi-step "glass skin" routinesSo, how best to look after teenage skin? Experts Dr Zainab Laftah and Dr Jonathan Kentley share their five top tips:Keep your skincare routine simple You need three basics: a gentle cleanser, a fragrance-free moisturiser and a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher. That's it.More skincare products aren't necessarily better A complicated routine with frequent exfoliations or strong acids can irritate young skin. Remember the skin barrier is still developing and it can result in damage. Dr Kently says he's seen an exponential rise in a condition called perioral dermatitis in teens, which is related to the overuse of ingredients that strip skin barriers like exfoliating hydroxy acids and retinoids. Dr Laftah adds: "Teens are increasingly adopting adult-style routines with numerous serums, toners, masks and actives. These actives are likely to result in skin barrier compromise and lead to more skin issues."Getting enough sleep and a balanced diet is important Raised cortisol through diets high in white carbohydrates and sugar as well as a lack of sleep have been linked to breakouts. Dr Laftah is a supporter of getting a good night's sleep. "We know that a lack of sleep increases cortisol levels, which is a stress hormone that can lead to acne breakouts." While Dr Kentley says a diet that is high in carbohydrate foods, like white rice and pasta, high sugar diets and whey protein found in protein shakes have all been linked in studies to acne flare-ups. But he makes the point that everyone's skin is individual and that "some people may find that other things flare up their skin".Don't pick or pop your spots The risk is that you can increase the inflammation by pushing the content deeper into the skin, which can result in scarring and discolouration. Dr Laftah says she's a fan of the pimple hydrocolloid star patches as a social media hack. "They work by absorbing fluid from superficial spots while creating a protective barrier that discourages picking," she explains.See a GP or dermatologist If you have persistent painful cystic or scarring acne, seek medical advice, as often prescription-grade treatment is needed.What about boys? A lot of the so-called "problems" during teenage years are related to androgens, a hormone which, although present in girls, is more prevalent in boys. "So male skin can sometimes be a little bit more oily and potentially have some more spots, and often you're getting to grips with the concept of facial hair and shaving, and that can introduce irritation," explains Dr Kentley."If you're not shaving properly you can develop quite a lot of folliculitis which is a bit of a crossover from acne. So you can cause quite a lot of damage to the skin barrier, a lot of inflammation."Here are Dr Kentley's top tips for shaving to protect skin:Shave after showering so that the skin is hot, has been steamed and prepared for a shaveUse a shaving brush to lift the hairs off the skinShave with something lubricating like shaving foam or shower gelAlways shave in the direction of travel of the hairs

schema.headline: The simple skincare routine for teens that actually works - and five expert tips

title: Andros Townsend: Being run over by pitch roller was terrifying
description: Former England winger Andros Townsend has described the moment he was run over by a pitch roller in Thailand as "terrifying".The 35‑year‑old former To
body: Former England winger Andros Townsend has described the moment he was run over by a pitch roller in Thailand as "terrifying".The 35‑year‑old former Tottenham, Luton and Crystal Palace forward, now with PT Prachuap in Thai League 1, was warming up for a match in Pattani on Saturday when a member of staff appeared to lose control of a heavy pitch roller.Townsend's left leg briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he was unhurt. He came off the bench late on in a 3-0 win.Speaking about the incident for the first time on Piers Morgan's Football Uncensored, Townsend said he was lucky to only escape from under the roller with a few "bumps and bruises"."Every time I see it, I'm cringing, I'm in disbelief," he said."It's horrible to watch back and to see what could have been."Thankfully I was fortunate I did manage to fall on to the floor at the right time, so nothing snapped as the roller went over me."Townsend, who won 13 caps for England, said he had thought it was strange to see two rollers either side of the pitch during the warm-up."I remember thinking to myself 'I've never seen that before in my career, what are they doing?' But we got called to warm-up. Didn't think anything [more] of it," he said."The next I saw him was when I was literally underneath him and thankfully no serious damage. A couple of bumps and bruises but managed to walk away unscathed, luckily."Townsend, who has had numerous setbacks with injuries during his career, said the roller incident was "definitely not going to stop me from continuing"."[My team-mates] were very surprised that I continued the warm-up. They were telling me to go to the doctor," he said."It was quite heavy, but I was able to kind of lift [it], force it off me. So when it was completely on me, I was getting crushed a little bit."I was able to get my left arm up and relieve some of the pressure, and then I was able to get my team-mates around me who were able to lift it, and I was able to squeeze out but at that moment where it was crushing my left leg, it was quite terrifying, I must say."Townsend was concerned his ankle and left knee, which have both been operated on, would be damaged in the incident.He said: "I thought either my left ankle was going to snap or my left knee is going to snap. I thought I was done. I was very fortunate that I was able to hobble away and recover within a few minutes."The midfielder made light of the incident on Instagram, referencing one of his recent posts in which he compared a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke's Bet365 Stadium.He wrote: "It turns out Stoke away wasn't so bad after all."

schema.headline: Andros Townsend: Being run over by pitch roller was terrifying

title: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly
description: Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement.The G7 also con
body: Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement.The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed pro-government forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security.Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the gateway to a key global shipping route.Iran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.The G7 statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to speak."We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.It went on: "Their reprehensible actions constitute a dangerous pattern of escalation that risks further exacerbating the conflict, undermining international trade and creating global economic instability.""Looking forward, we will continue to support the legitimate Government of Yemen and reaffirm our strong commitment to the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Yemen," the ministers said.Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.Meanwhile, at least six people were killed in Saudi strikes on the strategic Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mokha, the AFP news agency reported, citing Houthi-affiliated media.Two children and a woman were among the dead, while eight others were injured in the attack on the city, which the Houthis seized from pro-government forces earlier this month.Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government, has not yet commented on the reported strikes.The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast.Earlier this month, the Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen, took control of Bab al-Mandab, a narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region.The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.A diplomatic source told AFP that France has pledged support as well, and says is ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure via a "strictly defensive approach".Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported.Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday.The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran.On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified. The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement.Although Iran has denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN embargo, the UK and other Western powers have said their naval forces have repeatedly intercepted Iranian weapons shipments bound for Yemen during the civil war.A panel of UN experts also concluded in 2024 that the Houthis had been transformed into a powerful military organisation due to the transfer of materiel, assistance and training from Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Hezbollah and Iraqi specialists.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.Since taking control of Bab al-Mandab, they have said they pose no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

schema.headline: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly

title: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
description: Young people can book to get their Men B vaccine at high street pharmacies across England. There are walk-in appointments too, external. Two doses off
body: Young people can book to get their Men B vaccine at high street pharmacies across England. There are walk-in appointments too, external. Two doses offer the best protection. First doses are available until 31 December 2026, with second doses available until 31 March 2027. Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA, said: "This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change."The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place."Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer.Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before. These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added. Scientists say speed and severity of the Kent outbreak was very unusual. It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period.Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham.The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students.It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening. Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes.  Dr Rodrigues suspects the very same genetic changes that made the strain so dangerous may also explain why the outbreak was short-lived and did not continue to spread.People were generally too sick to be silent carriers who can pass it on unknowingly to others.Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn.Advisers, are asking the government to consider introducing MenB jabs routinely for secondary school-aged people at around the age of 15 to better protect them against a disease that can be deadly.

schema.headline: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe

title: Andy Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
description: Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.The prime minister and US p
body: Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship"."We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables."Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies. "The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."

schema.headline: Andy Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting

title: Bihar molestation case: India outrage after assault of teen girl and her friend in Jamui
description: A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread ou
body: A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage.The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave.The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene.Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects.The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities.The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them."The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action.Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration.Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible.Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral.The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police.Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage.Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl.A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso.Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention.Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people.Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added.The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together.Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers.Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel, external the incident had brought "shame to society". Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted.She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible.Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety.Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices"."This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter).Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state.Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action.India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation.The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy.The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.

schema.headline: Bihar molestation case: India outrage after assault of teen girl and her friend in Jamui

title: Luke Little booing row: Real fear darts superstar 'could walk away' from sport
description: At just 19, Luke Littler has won almost every major trophy in darts.He is a multi-millionaire with lucrative sponsorship deals and his own TV show.But
body: At just 19, Luke Littler has won almost every major trophy in darts.He is a multi-millionaire with lucrative sponsorship deals and his own TV show.But has his rapid rise turned some against him?This past weekend the teenager was once again subjected to boos and whistles from sections of the crowd as he took to the stage at the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam.What is surprising though is that it came as 'The Nuke' was on a quest to complete a darts clean sweep by becoming the first player to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year.Littler suggested afterwards that, if the booing continues, he will not attend events held in the Netherlands.But Samuel Gill, editor of Dartnews.com, suggests Littler's future in the sport could be at stake."There's a real fear that within a few years he'll just turn around and walk away from the sport," Gill told BBC Sport."So, I think for fans, 'Don't bite the hand that feeds you'. If people keep taunting him and don't want him to win, he might end up just walking away and not bothering anymore."Amsterdam was the latest tournament where Littler has faced what some might describe as an overly hostile reaction from fans.A vibrant pantomime-style atmosphere is part and parcel of the darts experience and Dutch and German crowds are amongs the most raucous - but it is clear Littler believes he has been unfairly targeted.The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last-16 on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed.It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday.The teenager's quarter-final defeat to Jonny Clayton ended Littler's quest for the clean sweep, but the Warrington native clearly felt fans had been unduly harsh towards him.Littler has now withdrawn from a series of upcoming events."Just no point in me travelling, wasting my time while I'm getting booed," said Littler.Littler has also been jeered at numerous events in the UK.His phenomenal rise saw him reach the PDC World Darts Championship aged just 16 in his debut year as a professional.He captured the title the following year and the trophies, sponsorship deals and six-figure winners' cheques have continued to flow.But increasingly so have whistles and boos during his performances."I don't think people expected him to reach the heights that he has so quickly," Gill said.The darts journalist - who became aware of Littler when the sport star was 14 - says this level of attention is not just unique to the British player."Michael van Gerwen was the same for a long time when he dominated the sport. He barely lost a game in about five years, and he was hoovering up titles for fun and it was similar," said Gill."Everyone wanted to boo him and even me as a viewer before I got into this role, growing up watching Van Gerwen, I wanted him to lose because it's something different for the sport every single week."Currently ranked number one in the world, Littler is so far ahead of his closest rivals that he already has the advantage of only having to play in selective tournaments.His boycott threat could end up being a blow to tournament organisers."They don't like him because he's that good. And he's got a bit of swagger to him," said Karl Holden secretary of St Helen's Darts Academy - where Littler honed his skills from the age of nine."Luke's got a bit of a character to him. For me, he's the ultimate professional. He might give a little bit of the large sometimes, but you need that, otherwise darts would be totally boring."It seems remarkable that the future of Littler's career in the sport is even being debated.More so when you consider his age and the fact he only turned professional two years ago.However, Gill believes that Littler's rapid haul of trophies, coupled with the huge amounts of money now in the sport, could result in the teenager leaving in the next "four to five years" should the boos and whistles continue.Gill believes Littler's impact on the darting world is immeasurable.Tickets to events featuring him are often sold out, applications to darting academies are reported to be at an all-time high and the Briton has transcended the sport.Gill therefore feels that, if Littler was to walk away, the sport would be the real loser."He's the one who is bringing this sport to a completely different level. Nowadays, he is back-page news wherever you go," Gill said."He might just decide 'I just want a quiet life now and just live off his money'."Littler has barely known anything other than winning. His challenged now is maintaining that victorious streak while keeping fans - whose interest helps fund his prize money - happy.Tricky when some are paying with the hope of seeing him lose."If he was on that stage, everybody liked him and he just threw darts, I think I'd get bored of watching him," Holden said.

schema.headline: Luke Little booing row: Real fear darts superstar 'could walk away' from sport

title: UK to help refuel Saudi jets countering Houthi attacks
description: Britain is set to deploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi Arabian fighter jets in the country's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen
body: Britain is set to deploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi Arabian fighter jets in the country's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.The RAF Voyager plane, operating from a UK base in Cyprus, will begin "air-to-air refuelling" operations in the coming days after the UK agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia, Defence Minister Luke Pollard said.He added the support was for "purely defensive" Saudi missions and would be time-limited for a "matter of weeks, rather than days".The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.In recent days, the Houthis in Yemen say they have carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.Explaining the nature of the deployment, Pollard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We've agreed to the Saudi request for air-to-air refuelling" that would keep Saudi jets "in the air longer"."The defensive action that Saudi Arabia takes against the Houthis will cover a range of activities, including shooting down those drones and missiles," he said.He insisted the UK support fully conformed with international humanitarian law, and was about "being true to our allies". The singular Voyager aircraft is part of a core fleet of nine - eight military registered and another civilian registered - on the Royal Air Force (RAF)'s books.The RAF also has five others available for military recall if needed.Speaking to reporters travelling with him on the way to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Burnham linked cost of living pressures to the decision."I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region," he said."Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request."Pollard added the UK support would "ensure there's not further escalation in the Red Sea, which could further risk our fuel prices".Petrol prices in the UK jumped to their highest for nearly four years in August, the Office for National Statistics said, while diesel also rocketed.Shipping routes through the Red Sea are a vital artery of the world economy.The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to the Red Sea - a key shipping route used by Saudi Arabia.As "military support" goes, Britain's offer of a single Voyager refuelling aircraft is at the lighter end of the spectrum. Some may even see this as a performative gesture to an ally in trouble.Saudi Arabia is struggling to fend off attacks by Yemen's Houthis who seem to have an inexhaustible supply of drones and missiles to fire at their large and vulnerable Saudi neighbour to the north.British officials have said this offer is, as they put it, "time-limited".But Yemen has been at war, on and off, since 2014 and this latest upsurge in fighting is made more complicated by the fact the Houthis are backed by Iran which is in its own on-off war with the US.The risk for Britain here is limited but wars have a habit of drawing nations in with a steadily increasing involvement. That may well suit the Saudis but it is unlikely to please most people in Britain.In a BBC interview last week, Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte hinted that European support for Saudi Arabia was also likely.He said: "I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'."Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful."Energy Minister Martin McCluskey last week told MPs that the UK was "providing air defence support" to Saudi Arabia through the defence partnership that they have, although would not be drawn on questions of operational military activity.In January 2024, the UK joined the US in launching air strikes against Houthi targets across Yemen.Then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said the UK "acted in self-defence" following the Houthis' targeting of ships, including a Royal Navy warship.He also said the strikes were "necessary, proportionate, and targeted" to protect lives and commercial shipping.Further joint air strikes from the UK and US followed in 2024, external.

schema.headline: UK to help refuel Saudi jets countering Houthi attacks

title: What we found in Earl Spencer's controversial Diana memoir
description: The coverage has been driven by a simple question: should we believe Earl Spencer's claims about the King's callousness after Diana's death? Or should
body: The coverage has been driven by a simple question: should we believe Earl Spencer's claims about the King's callousness after Diana's death? Or should we believe the unusually robust denial from Buckingham Palace?But when you read further through the book, there's a more complicated story being told.Earl Spencer is the brother watching events unfolding in the strange and ultimately doomed life of his sister, who has stepped from being his childhood companion to become one of the most famous women in the world.He describes a kind of grief and irritation as Diana becomes public property and then royal property, which irks him even more, disliking the "nonsense of fawning" around the monarchy.It's a stark reminder that Diana was only just 20 years old when she married - becoming a global superstar - and was dead 16 years later.Earl Spencer depicts her as a caring, generous character who was haunted by self-doubt, dogged by eating disorders, lacking in warmth from her new royal family and then ultimately dragged down by the tabloid media."She craved acceptance, admiration, kindness, and - perhaps above all - love," writes Charles Spencer about Diana."She got stuck into gritty, controversial, but crucial causes partly because she had a fine, natural social conscience, but also to assuage nagging feelings of worthlessness."And with a memoir like this it will be the extra details that will fascinate people.The stepmother to Diana and Charles, Raine Spencer, is painted in an unflattering light, and Diana is described as getting so angry once that she pushed Raine down the staircase at their home in Althorp. "Raine fortunately landed flush on her buttocks, rather than on bone, and got up, leaving the saloon without a backwards glance," he writes. It was in response, says the book, to Raine telling Diana: "I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying someone quite as stupid as you."There's not a single mention of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, even though she was talked about in the TV interviewsWe're told that a "nephew" wanted Earl Spencer to be in a documentary about Diana, which will raise speculation about Prince Harry's plans for his mother's 30th anniversary next yearThe book recounts that she disliked Dodi Fayed's father, Mohammed Fayed, accusing him of crudely groping herDiana's preferences included the soap opera Crossroads and the music of David Bowie. She'd watched The Sound of Music 16 times and the paper she read was the Daily MailEarl Spencer will ultimately be remembered by the passionate eulogy he delivered at Diana's funeral in Westminster Abbey.He reveals how he had pretended to have lost his copy of his speech at the rehearsal, so no one could hear it in advance and try to tone down his stinging criticism of the press and the royals.After the hounding of Diana by the paparazzi, he says he personally rang tabloid newspaper editors to disinvite them from the Abbey funeral, after their invitations had already been sent out.She was buried on an island in the Spencers' Althorp estate, rather than a graveyard - and the book describes how a bishop was brought to consecrate the ground to make it possible.Much of the interest in this book has been driven by its settling of old scores with the Royal Family. It can feel like medieval barons jousting.References to King Charles are almost all negative, including the suggestion that he was jealous of his wife's public popularity.The book reports a conversation in which it's claimed the then-Prince Charles complained: "I mean, I'm 43,' he said, 'and I employ fifty people' – he was flushed in the face now – 'but my parents insist on treating me like – like a child!'"The King is portrayed as resentful, with a "senior courtier" reporting an alleged comment by the late Queen: "He even resented it when I taught him the alphabet."There's a bizarre account of discussions in the Royal Family about whether the then-Prince Charles's ears should have been pinned back.And there's the allegation that Diana had said the King was in love with his valet, which the author himself says seemed improbable.What comes across is how close the Spencers were to the royals - but without being friends. Charles and Diana Spencer went to the same children's parties as the young royals.The royals are depicted as the type of children who come round, break your toys and then disappear, in what might be an extended metaphor for how he saw Diana's story.There's also a story about a teenage Prince Andrew smirking in a church service because the priest used the word "womb".While the TV interviews have sought Spencer's views on Prince Harry and Prince William, the book doesn't go there.Earl Spencer describes his opposition to the boys having to walk behind the coffin at their mother's funeral - and he talks of "how tiny, and slight, and bereft, Harry looked".But the focus of this book is much more about the Diana era - and an elegy to the lost world of their childhood.Earl Spencer emphasises its country house happiness, with dens, dogs and horses, but it's also dotted with cruelty, with violent nannies and the "mindless and often destructive" tradition of boarding schools.A boy who accidentally shot and killed his father gets the mawkish nickname "Baghdad".Although the book is about Diana, it's also about its author, the younger brother trying to make sense of what's happened - and also, like many younger brothers, being able to criticise without being able to take responsibility.Earl Spencer talks about how little he cares for "archaic" titles for the aristocracy or royals.And in this book, the title that seems really to have shaped his life most is "Diana's brother".Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, by Charles Spencer. Published by Penguin.

schema.headline: What we found in Earl Spencer's controversial Diana memoir

title: Martha's Rule rolled out across all A&E departments in England
description: The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek second opin
body: The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek second opinions about their care if they want. It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 at King's College Hospital in London in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule. Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being listened to.The nationwide expansion starts now and should be complete by March 2028, following a successful trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out across all inpatient wards.Prof Aidan Fowler, national director of patient safety at NHS England, said the expansion of Martha's Rule would give families and NHS staff "a critical new lifeline" to help improve care and save more lives.Prof Fowler told the BBC that a Martha's Rule call would mean a patient receives an "appropriate response", for example, a senior nurse or member of the critical care outreach team could conduct a review of the case.Staff can themselves also ask for a review from a different team if they are concerned the appropriate action is not being taken.During an eight-month pilot of the scheme at seven emergency departments, 69 calls were made to dedicated Martha's Rule phone numbers, including some calls relating to acute deterioration following an urgent clinical review. In some cases, it led to a patient having immediate surgery or being transferred to intensive care.Prof Fowler told the BBC's Today programme that, while these numbers might seem relatively small, the decision to roll out Martha's Rule further "is on a background of very, very extensive experience in other settings". This included in-patient wards, where Prof Fowler said his teams had received "nearly 20,000 calls"; three quarters of which came from families.Prof Fowler said: "Early testing has shown that Martha's Rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children's wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date, with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions."Questioned whether busy A&E staff might struggle with a sudden influx of calls, Prof Fowler told the BBC this had not played out in the recent tests. "There was a concern we would receive an overwhelming number of calls, and that would be a distraction and actually divert staff from the important work they're doing," he said. "But that hasn't been the case, actually people have used it very sensibly," he added. "We've tested it through winter and across this busy summer and therefore I am not concerned that when we roll this out we are going to be overwhelmed with calls." Health minister Baroness Merron said the initiative was part of "wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS."Scotland is beginning to use Martha's Rule and Northern Ireland is considering using it, while Wales has a similar scheme called Call4Concern.Actor Jason Watkins, whose two-and-a-half-year-old daughter Maude died from sepsis in 2011, praised the rollout, saying Martha's rule "is making a difference on the wards"."It enables a parent to have a voice and if there is an issue, that is addressed," he told BBC Breakfast, and urged parents: "if you're at all worried when you go into A&E, ask for a second opinion."Watkins said the rollout of Martha's law could benefit medical professionals too, explaining: "Those extremely dedicated medical practitioners, nurses, doctors and consultants, it gives them a pause and a thought 'am I doing everything I can to assess this child accurately?'".The phased rollout in England will be completed by March 2028.Patients and their families can check with their local hospital or NHS trust where Martha's Rule is available by visiting the trust's website or asking hospital staff.

schema.headline: Martha's Rule rolled out across all A&E departments in England

title: Vet prescription fees to be capped under rule changes
description: Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at £21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the co
body: Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at £21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the coming months.Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online, write price estimates ahead of treatment, and publish price lists for services as part of the rule updates.The official competition watchdog has brought the measures into force after its investigation into the sector found prices had been rising at nearly twice the rate of inflation.However, critics say the measures will hit independent vets hardest and will benefit the six firms that own more than two-thirds of practices.The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) made its remedies for the sector legally binding as of Tuesday and vets have up to 12 months to bring all the changes in.As well as capping prescription fees, other changes include:Vet practices must publish a "comprehensive" price list for standard services – including consultations, common procedures, and cremation optionsA written estimate must be provided in advance for any treatment expected to cost £500 or more, including aftercare costs, plus an itemised bill. Emergencies are the only exception to thisVet businesses must make clear whether they are part of a group or an independent businessTo help pet owners compare local practices, price and ownership information will be made available through the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons' "Find a Vet" service, which will share the data with third-party comparison sites.The timelines for when vets need to bring in the fixes depends on the exact regulation and the group's size. The CMA sets it out here., external"The changes that are being required are changes that will help inform pet owners about prices," said CMA panel chair Martin Coleman.However, Cate Titterton, the owner of an independent vet service in Saltburn, told the BBC the changes will make trips to the vets more expensive for customers."Veterinary practices still have to have a pharmacy that is fully stocked, so if we're not making that tiny profit on the drugs, we're going to have to make some profit elsewhere."So, things like services, consultations, surgeries – unfortunately, those prices are very, very likely to have to go up."She believes there is "one clear winner" from this - larger vet groups and the corporates.File on 4 Investigates: What's Happening to Your Vet Bills?Cat Henstridge, another vet, said it was "wonderful" that businesses must now make clear if they are part of a large group, but noted that such groups "have not actually been asked to change their ownership of any clinics or anything like that".Speaking on the Today programme, she advised pet owners who are worried about the cost of care to "be open and honest with your vet about what is affordable for you"."There is always going to be a bill. Veterinary medicine is private medicine. Owning a pet does come with the responsibility of paying for their care. "[By] working with us, we can make it work for you, but you have to tell us about it first," she said.British Veterinary Association President Dr Rob Williams said veterinary practices were already largely working to the CMA's remedies, including the orders relating to complaints handling, price estimates for routine procedures and prescription costs."We've been clear with the CMA throughout its investigation that it must ensure its remedies do not disproportionately impact smaller, independent practices and we've pushed back where we've had concerns," Williams said.

schema.headline: Vet prescription fees to be capped under rule changes

title: Henry Pollock: England flanker extends deal with Northampton
description: Henry Pollock has brought an end to his contract stand-off with Northampton, saying it was ultimately "a very easy decision" to sign an extension with
body: Henry Pollock has brought an end to his contract stand-off with Northampton, saying it was ultimately "a very easy decision" to sign an extension with the defending Prem champions."I am very, very happy to sign here," Pollock told BBC Radio Northampton."I have been here my whole career so it made sense for me to stay on the journey with such a young group of players, who are so ambitious."It was a very easy decision in the end."The 21-year-old, whose profile has exploded over the past two seasons after appearing for England and the British and Irish Lions, had been talked up as a "seven-figure player" during negotiations by his advisor Eddie Hearn.However, the boxing promoter's valuation was never likely to be met at Northampton or elsewhere in the Prem, given Saints' star-studded line-up, the league's £6.4m squad salary cap and rules over players moving between clubs.The exact level of Pollock's pay increase is unclear. While some sources have valued his new contract at £400,000 a year, others involved in the deal say the figure is higher.It is certainly short of Scotland playmaker Finn Russell, who, as Bath's marquee player, is on the league's most lucrative package, worth about £1m a year.Pollock's pay puts him well ahead of most of his contemporaries in the Prem however.His new deal is comfortably ahead of the average annual salary in the league (£191,000), the average earned by someone in his 20-22 age bracket (£106,000) and with his level of international experience (£224,000), as revealed by the latest league payroll data, covering the 2024-25 campaign., externalOnly 4% of Prem players that season were paid in excess of £400,000 a year.Pollock's previous contract, signed in December 2024, is understood to have been worth about £150,000.Northampton say his new deal is a "multi-year" agreement that keeps him at the club beyond the expiry of his previous contract in summer 2027."I don't create it, my team do," said Pollock of the speculation that has surrounded his future over the past seven weeks."It is one of those things that you have to take in your stride, but I am happy it is all done and I can focus on the rugby."Asked about the possibility of Saints becoming the first side since Saracens in 2019 to successfully defend their English title, Pollock was bullish."We have the squad depth and the belief in this group that we can do it," he said."Let's see, hopefully we can create some magic along the way. Let's write a new story."Pollock, who was instrumental in Northampton's run to the title last season, insisted last week that he was still open to offers, raising the possibility of a move abroad or even to another sport.However, remaining at Northampton, for whom he made his league debut in November 2023, always seemed the most likely option.After winning an age-grade world title with England's under-20s at the end of that season, Pollock returned to Franklin's Gardens and established himself as a first-team regular.His pace, energy and on-pitch persona propelled him into the public consciousness and into contention for international honours. He made his Test debut off the bench against Wales, scoring two tries, in March 2025 and was a bolter pick for the Lions squad only two months later.His try-scoring feats through Saints' run to the Champions Cup final, complete with pre-planned celebrations, earned him a spot on the eight-strong shortlist for the continental competition's player of the year.He has appeared in each of England's past 12 Tests, albeit with his only start coming in a 42-21 defeat by Ireland in February."Over the last few years, everyone has seen the quality he brings on the pitch and the speed of his rise through the game – but just as importantly, he's a young man of outstanding character," said Northampton's director of rugby Phil Dowson."What's most exciting is that there's still so much more to come from him. Henry is incredibly ambitious and constantly looking for ways to improve. He understands that individual success comes from contributing to a successful team, and he's already taken on leadership responsibilities within the squad despite his age."People sometimes underestimate how intelligent he is as a rugby player. When we sit down to review performances, he's often identified the same things we were going to discuss before we've even raised them. His understanding of the game is excellent, and that gives him a huge platform to keep progressing."He's become an important figure not just for Saints, but for the wider game. He inspires young supporters, brings excitement to rugby, and understands that everything off the pitch is built on performing consistently on it. We're excited to see what he can achieve over the coming years."

schema.headline: Henry Pollock: England flanker extends deal with Northampton

title: Flight disruption: Airlines criticise air traffic control over second glitch in a month
description: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.EasyJ
body: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the service, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.Nats said a "connectivity issue" at Prestwick was behind the disruption across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England - and had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick earlier this month.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said further issues today "cause even greater concern" about the UK's air traffic control.When asked by reporters whether he would look to fire the head of Nats, Burnham said "these are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated".He added that the transport secretary was taking the issues "extremely seriously" and initially it's a matter for her "to get to the bottom of... and why there has been a recurrence."The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity", although officials warned of knock-on effects.A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".More than 150 flights were cancelled at UK airports on Monday - including 140 departures and 137 arrivals, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 48 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 13 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".An independent review by the CAA into the resilience of the UK's air traffic control system is under way and the results will be published "within six months", it said.Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure". Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership.Asked on BBC Radio 4's World at One programme if Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?"Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure.Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers.British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing".A Nats spokesperson apologised, saying: "In the real world, we accept technology can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible."What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority."They added that it was working to return air traffic to normal as quickly as possible and urged passengers to check their flight status with their airline.Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the situation was "deeply frustrating" for passengers. Steve Davies, 74, told the BBC he was "cheesed off with air traffic control" as technical issues with its systems seemed to be "happening a lot".He and his wife Sadie became stuck at Birmingham airport after being told to disembark their EasyJet flight to Edinburgh on Monday morning.Nicole McCloskey, from Kilmarnock, had been due to go to Disneyland Paris with her family before their flight was cancelled.She told the BBC her family got a message to say the flight was delayed while they were travelling to Glasgow airport, but only found out it had been grounded altogether once they arrived.Nicole said they have been rebooked on another flight on later on Monday and were hopeful "it's sorted in time".

schema.headline: Flight disruption: Airlines criticise air traffic control over second glitch in a month

title: Inside Scotland's wildcat HQ - 'It's like Big Brother for cats'
description: Image source, Saving WildcatsImage caption, The project has released 46 wildcats into the foothills of the CairngormsByScotland correspondentFrom behi
body: Image source, Saving WildcatsImage caption, The project has released 46 wildcats into the foothills of the CairngormsByScotland correspondentFrom behind a giant bank of screens in a small windowless room, Estelle Morgan, animal team leader from the Saving Wildcats partnership, is keeping an eye on the latest wildcats being bred in captivity for release into the Cairngorms."It's like Big Brother for cats", she says of the 72 cameras being used to watch over the animals in their enclosures.They are assessing whether they're healthy and have the behavioural potential to survive in the wild."We want to know what the cats are actually doing," she says.Image caption, Estelle Morgan monitors the wildcats via 72 cameras in the Cairngorms"What are they like without us there? she adds. "Are they able to climb? Are they able to pounce? Can they navigate complex structures? Are they active at natural times?" This year they were even able to capture on camera for the first time a wildcat giving birth.It is quite a surveillance programme - but it has to be. They don't want the cats to become comfortable around people and contact is kept to an absolute minimum.They are also assessing the cats' behaviour ahead of being released: "If we've got some cats which are quite bold does that mean they're more likely to go near roads in the wild, or venture closer to a farm or to human settlements," she says.Image source, Saving WildcatsImage caption, For the first time this year, Saving Wildcats were able to observe a wildcat having its kittensSaving Wildcats has been successful in reintroducing 46 wildcats into the flats and foothills of the Cairngorms.Those wildcats have successfully reproduced and the team working on the project are aware of at least 20 wild-born litters to released females since 2024.There are now plans to reintroduce wildcat populations into other areas in Scotland.The Cairngorm project has had "an enormous amount of success, but it is only the first step," says NatureScot species project manager Dr Martin Gaywood.Now he says they need to think big: "Wildcat conservation is really complex. It has all sorts of threats and issues and in order to restore wildcats to the whole of Scotland we need to plan long term and we need to plan at a big scale."Dr Gaywood is optimistic that with careful planning the translocation of wildcats into other parts of Scotland could happen within years: "It would be great maybe within the next five years to start at least one new project, you never know maybe two," he says.Image caption, Helen Senn said climate incidents had the potential to have an impact on the wildcat conservation programmeAs well as identifying new release sites, the national strategy will prioritise restoring and reconnecting wildcat habitats to allow the expansion of their range.In the areas chosen for the eventual translocation of wildcat populations there will be additional microchipping, neutering and vaccination of pet and feral cats to reduce interbreeding.Dr Helen Senn, head of conservation and science at the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland (RZSS), says climate change is one of the reasons why is it important to  identify other areas in which wildcat populations can be reintroduced."We have had some really big climate incidents here in the Strath over the last couple of years. "We've had some major storms and flooding incidents. We've also had, unfortunately, a very significant forest fire in the north of the release area and all of these have the potential to impact the population".She adds: "The way to be resilient to risk is to have larger population sizes and to have populations present in multiple areas".Image caption, Louise Hughes leads the team that tracks the wildcats as they establish their new territoriesIn 2018, scientists warned that the Scottish wildcat population was functionally extinct. They are classed as critically endangered so even once released the wildcats that now roam the Cairngorms are still carefully monitored.A network of trail cameras - up to 100 at any one time - captures their movements.  The wildcats are also fitted with collars which drop off after around seven to nine months in the wild which emit a signal for a short period of time every day. Louise Hughes, who is operations manager for the Saving Wildcats partnership, explains that the information they are gathering is invaluable, although not always easy to pick up. She says the wildcats establishing their new territories: "Might be down a hole, they might be in a tree root, they might have gone for a wander over the mountains."But the data can help the scientists learn more about the cats' movements and hunting behaviour. It can also help them understand the habitat the wildcats are using.'Sully is an amazing cat'Scottish Land and Estates has been supportive of the Scottish Wildcat Conservation Action Plan. Several estates have been actively helping: providing release sites, monitoring the wildcats, recording sightings.Lots of the information being gathered does come from public sightings. Louise takes me to the territory on which one wildcat that was recently captured on camera:  "The cat that lives in this territory, Sully, is an amazing cat. She was released in 2024 and she has been captured on video swimming across the River Spey." Wildcats, she says, "never cease to surprise us."Estelle Morgan points out that wildcats were once widespread throughout the UK.The work they are doing in the Cairngorms will help inform releases elsewhere in Scotland. She says the only native cat found in the wild in Britain "deserves to be here, they're part of the landscape."

schema.headline: Inside Scotland's wildcat HQ - 'It's like Big Brother for cats'
